title: Zeus's one gift
hookLine: the gods gave us one thing wholly ours: the right use of impressions (Discourses 1.1)
carry: only the use of impressions is wholly mine

lines: SPELL-CHECK CAN'T TELL YOU TO SEND IT.
EVERY TOOL IS SILENT ABOUT SOMETHING.
cards: Spell-check can tell you a word is misspelled. It can't tell you whether to send the email. A music app can tell you the song is in the right key.
It can't tell you whether this is the moment to sing it. Each tool judges its own work and goes quiet on whether to use it.
The very first discourse in the book opens with the same observation, using the tools of Epictetus' day. Then it asks: so what in us can answer the real question?

teach.h: GRAMMAR CAN'T SAY WHETHER TO WRITE.
teach.b: Look at all the skills and faculties, Epictetus says, and you won't find one that examines itself. Grammar can judge what's written, but if you're writing to a friend, grammar won't tell you whether to write.
Music can judge a tune, but not whether to sing or play right now. What will tell you?
The faculty that examines itself and everything else: reason. Only it asks what it is, what it can do, and what it's worth. Gold doesn't tell you gold is beautiful.
Something in you does, by how it uses the impression of gold.

So the gods, Epictetus says, put in our power only the best thing, the ruler of all the rest: the right use of impressions. Everything else they left outside our power. Then he imagines Zeus explaining himself.
If I could have, Zeus says, I would have made your body and your little property free too. But your body isn't really yours. It's clay, cleverly mixed.

teach.h: ZEUS: I GAVE YOU A PART OF MYSELF.
teach.b: Since I couldn't, I gave you a part of myself: this power to choose and refuse, to desire and avoid, to use impressions. Look after it, and you'll never be blocked.
You might believe in Zeus, in God, in nature, in evolution, or in none of these, and the point still lands. You didn't get to choose most of what happens.
You did get one thing that's wholly yours: what you do with how things appear to you. An impression arrives: they're ignoring me. You get to examine it before you agree.
That's the gift, and it's yours by use, not by owning it.

how: People practicing Stoicism often pause on a strong first impression, such as an insult or a fear, and examine whether it is true before acting on it, which Epictetus calls the right use of impressions.

games.q: what does “the gift of use” mean?
o: the right use of impressions, the one thing wholly ours
a talent you're born with and should never waste
the gods' gift of a healthy, useful body

games.q: the gift of use — tap the pairs.

s: in Discourses 1.1, Zeus says the body is truly ours
he says it isn't ours: it's clay, cleverly mixed.
Epictetus says only reason examines itself
grammar and music judge their own fields, but not whether to use them.

games.q: you're about to send an angry email. spell-check says it's perfect. what does Epictetus say decides whether to send it?
o: the faculty that examines impressions: reason.
how the other person will react.
games.why: grammar can't tell you whether to write. only the faculty that uses impressions can, and it's the one thing wholly yours.

practice: Let the sounds of the room come to you, a car, a fan, a voice next door, and notice the comment that arrives with each one: annoying, nice, too loud. For each, see two things: the sound, and then my take on it.
You don't have to change the take; seeing it as a take is the use.

wordCard.voice: The gift of use. Discourses one, chapter one: the one thing wholly ours is the right use of impressions. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an impression or appearance, what the mind is given to use well.

carryVoice: Your line: only the use of impressions is wholly mine. Grammar can't say whether to write; you can. That's three hundred eighty-nine.
